meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The next flag they plant will be all white, and it'll be surrender'?
meta.ogDescription: Michigan State planted a flag at midfield in Notre Dame Stadium. Notre Dame’s former coach, newly hired at ESPN, had a suggestion for the next one.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1937–2026 · college football coach; Notre Dame national champion, 1988
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Holtz, and entirely in character for him: on 17 September 2005 Michigan State beat Notre Dame 44–41 in overtime and planted a Spartan flag on the Notre Dame Stadium turf, and Holtz — Notre Dame’s head coach from 1986 to 1996, by then in his first season as an ESPN analyst — was asked about it. But the only citation anyone offers is a Sports Illustrated column two days later whose web address is dead, and we could not read the archived copy. We have not confirmed the wording against a source we could open.

source.excerpt: “The next flag they plant will be all white, and it’ll be surrender.”
trail: Wikiquote ↗ files this line under Attributed, which is its own signal: the page has no sourced section at all, and every quotation on it carries the same kind of second-hand citation.

The citation it does give is John Walters, “Cool Hand on the remote,” SportsIllustrated.com, 19 September 2005. The host sportsillustrated.cnn.com no longer resolves. An archived capture is recorded in the Wayback Machine, but web.archive.org is blocked from our network, so we have not read the column and are not counting it as corroboration.

The occasion, however, is solid. Michigan State’s 2005 schedule ↗ records a 44–41 overtime win at Notre Dame Stadium on 17 September 2005 over the tenth-ranked Irish, and Wikipedia’s article on flag planting ↗ names that game as one of the era’s flag-planting incidents: Michigan State players planted their flag on Notre Dame’s field. The column Wikiquote cites is dated two days later.

Holtz was well placed to be asked. His biography ↗ has him coaching Notre Dame from 1986 to 1996 and working as an ESPN college-football analyst from 2005 until 2015 — so in September 2005 he was a first-season broadcaster commenting on his old programme being humiliated at home.

A phrase search across the whole of English Wikiquote returns only the Lou Holtz page for this sentence. That is a meaningful negative in one direction — nobody else is claiming it — and no help in the other, because an uncontested attribution is still an unsourced one.

author.name: Lou Holtz
author.heading: About Lou Holtz
author.metaLine: 1937–2026 · American college football coach · Notre Dame, 1986–1996
author.bio: Lou Holtz was an American college football coach who led six different programmes to bowl games — William & Mary, North Carolina State, Arkansas, Minnesota, Notre Dame and South Carolina — and finished with a career college record of 249–132–7. His 1988 Notre Dame team went 12–0 and was the consensus national champion. He was elected to the College Football Hall of Fame in 2008 and worked as a television analyst for CBS and then ESPN, where the one-liners that fill his quotation pages mostly come from.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Planting a flag on a beaten opponent’s field was still a rare provocation in 2005, and Notre Dame Stadium was a pointed place to try it. Michigan State had just won there 44–41 in overtime, against a team ranked tenth in the country, and drove their Spartan flag into the turf in front of 80,795 people.

Holtz had spent eleven seasons as Notre Dame’s head coach and won the programme its most recent national championship. He was in his first season as a television analyst. The line does the two things his reputation was built on at once: it defends his old school and it gets the laugh.
detailsBody: The joke has aged into something close to prophecy, which is part of why it still circulates: flag-planting went from an oddity to a recurring flashpoint in college football over the following two decades, eventually drawing brawls, a Nick Saban condemnation and a proposed Ohio law.

It is worth being clear about what is and is not established here. The game, the flag and Holtz’s position at the microphone are all documented. The sentence itself is not — it rests on a single column nobody can currently open. On a site about provenance that distinction is the whole point, so we have marked the line attributed rather than verified.

Lou Holtz (January 6, 1937 – March 4, 2026) was head coach at Notre Dame 1986–1996, his 1988 team was consensus national champion, and he worked as a TV college football analyst for ESPN from 2005 until 2015.
The 2005 Michigan State schedule records an away game at Notre Dame Stadium on September 17 against tenth-ranked Notre Dame, won 44–41 in overtime, attendance 80,795.
Wikipedia’s "Flag planting" article states that flag-planting incidents in college football included Michigan State players planting their flag on Notre Dame’s field in 2005.
